common_name: Bonnie and Clyde Sedge (Mop-Top Howe's Sedge)

planting.note: Divide and transplant in spring or early fall; keep soil consistently moist until established.

directions: A fine-textured, mounding sedge native to boggy meadows and swamp-forest stream banks from Maine to Texas, forming a tidy mop-top clump of thread-like green leaves. Grow in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil along pond edges, rain gardens, or woodland seeps. Pair with hostas or heucheras for textural contrast and allow space for gentle self-seeding in favorable sites. Needs little maintenance beyond an early-spring tidy-up of old foliage.

common_name: Willow the Wisp Sedge (Hair-Fine Howe's Sedge)

planting.note: Plant in consistently damp to wet soil; tolerates standing water once established.

directions: An exceptionally fine, weeping-textured selection of a wetland native sedge found in blackwater streams from Michigan to Florida and Texas, making it one of the most wet-tolerant sedges in cultivation. Site it at pond margins, rain gardens, or anywhere soil stays saturated, where its cascading hair-like foliage softens bolder companions. Needs minimal care beyond occasional division to control spread and a spring cleanup of winter-worn blades.

planting.note: Plant in humus-rich soil with half-day sun; established clumps tolerate considerably drier, shadier spots.

directions: A large, evergreen southern native sedge grown for its graceful, pendant flowering stems that arch outward from the clump in spring, resembling tan-and-cream tassels. Best sited where it gets morning sun and afternoon shade, though it handles dry shade better than most moisture-loving sedges once established. Good as a bold accent in rain gardens or woodland borders, and pollinators work the early blooms readily.

planting.note: Grow in average to consistently moist soil; a southern-sourced selection with good heat tolerance.

directions: A semi-evergreen selection of white-tinged sedge, a wide-ranging North American woodland native, chosen from a southern Texas population for extra heat and humidity tolerance. Forms a dense clump topped in spring by gracefully arching flower stalks that drape over the foliage mound. Useful as a groundcover or rock-garden filler in part-shade borders where summer heat limits other sedges, and tolerates both average garden soil and damp shade.

common_name: Miss Mississippi Sedge (Compact Woodland Groundcover Sedge)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich woodland soil; a recent selection from a Gulf South forest population.

directions: A neat, evergreen mounding sedge native to moist forests from Maryland to Florida and west to Texas, valued for its tidy habit and medium-width, arching foliage. Thrives in part sun to light shade with reliably moist, well-drained soil, making it a good companion for ferns and hostas in woodland plantings. Low-maintenance once established, it spreads slowly by division rather than seeding aggressively.

planting.note: Adaptable to a wide range of soils, from dry roadside banks to seasonally flooded low ground.

directions: A widespread but underused North American native sedge selected for its fine, narrow foliage that cascades into a waterfall-shaped clump, with slender seed spikes rising well above the leaves in early summer. Remarkably adaptable, tolerating both dry sites and periodically wet lowground, and largely ignored by deer and rabbits. Works well in rain gardens, rock gardens, or naturalistic prairie-edge plantings where low water sedges are needed.

planting.note: Tolerates average garden soil with regular watering despite its dry-prairie origin.

directions: Native to dry, sandy prairies mostly east of the Mississippi, this selection forms a wide, evergreen mound of narrow leaves that arch outward well beyond the crown. Garden plants adapt readily to amended, irrigated soils despite their drought-tolerant prairie origin, making this a flexible choice for rain gardens or looser, naturalistic borders. Light spring flowers in tan and cream add subtle seasonal interest, and the clump resists both deer and rabbit browsing.

planting.note: Plant in rich, moist woodland soil; divide established clumps in early fall or spring.

directions: A selection of the broad-leaved eastern woodland sedge, chosen for wide, glossy, seersucker-textured leaves that hold their good looks after flowering rather than fading. Native from Canada south to northern Alabama, it thrives in rich, consistently moist woodland soil under high shade and stays evergreen in milder climates. An excellent slow-spreading groundcover beneath native understory shrubs, ferns, and wildflowers.

planting.note: Plant in consistently moist to wet soil; suited to bog edges and rain gardens.

directions: A variegated selection of the circumboreal black sedge, bearing fine light-green leaves edged in gold that form a low, spreading, arching mat. Naturally found in wet meadows and streambanks, it performs best in evenly moist to wet soil and part sun to shade, where its color is brightest. Tiny near-black flower spikes appear in spring. A good choice for pond margins, rain gardens, or as a woodland groundcover, and it is largely ignored by rabbits.

planting.note: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in light shade; a slow, well-behaved spreader.

directions: A diminutive European spring sedge selection with dark, near-black-green leaves narrowly edged in gold, giving a striped mop-top effect close to the ground. Forms a dense, slow-spreading, evergreen tuft that works well tucked between stepping stones or massed as a fine-textured groundcover in light shade. Prefers consistently moist soil but adapts to somewhat drier conditions once established, and its restrained spread makes it easy to keep in bounds.

planting.note: Grow in moist to wet soil along pond edges, rain gardens, or moist woodland beds.

directions: A German-raised selection of the native palm sedge, named for its upright, sentinel-like stems that carry whorled, palm-frond-like leaf arrangements. Native to floodplain woods of the central and eastern United States, it spreads readily in moist to wet soil and is a reliable choice for rain gardens, pond margins, and damp shade borders. Rabbit-resistant and easy to divide, it combines well with ferns and broad-leaved shade perennials.
